# Why won't my engine rotate?

If you've just replaced a rear main seal and an intermediate shaft bearing on a 911, only to find the crankshaft refuses to turn past 150 degrees of rotation, you are likely facing a classic interference scenario. The fact that you can rotate the engine manually with a wrench on the flywheel but hit a hard stop suggests mechanical binding rather than a seized component.

The core issue here is almost certainly valve-to-piston contact. When rotating an internal combustion engine to check static timing, you must ensure the pistons are in their lowest point (Bottom Dead Center) while the valves are closed. If any cylinder is at Top Dead Center (TDC) on a compression or exhaust stroke while you try to rotate it, the camshafts will have pushed the intake or exhaust valves open into the path of the rising piston.

You noted that you used a borescope and saw clearance between the pistons and valves in some cylinders. This observation is expected but can be misleading if you assume it applies to all cylinders at that specific crank angle. In an interference engine like the 3.4L air-cooled Porsche, the timing chain has slack, or the sprockets have slipped relative to each other, causing the camshafts to open valves when they shouldn't. Even a slight misalignment of the timing chainâperhaps just a few teeth off on the crankshaft sprocket or an intermediate shaft jumpâcan shift the valve events enough to cause contact.

The critical detail you mentioned is that the cam-locking procedure was not followed prior to removing components, and the cams are currently unsecured. Without locking tools or a method to physically hold the camshafts in place, rotating the engine risks catastrophic damage if you inadvertently turn it into a TDC position. Rotating backwards is also risky; unless you are certain the timing marks align perfectly with zero degrees on both crank and cam sprockets, reverse rotation can push valves open against closed pistons just as effectively as forward rotation.

To diagnose this without stripping the engine further, you need to identify which cylinder(s) are currently in an interference position. Since you cannot rely on visual inspection alone through a borescope at a single static angle, the most reliable method is to locate Top Dead Center on the crankshaft sprocket and verify the camshaft positions simultaneously.

If you can remove the timing covers and access the timing chain tensioners and sprockets, look closely at the alignment of the timing marks. On these 3.4L engines, the intermediate shaft bearing sits just below the main crankshaft bearing at the rear of the engine. If the intermediate shaft bearing was damaged during the seal replacement or if the set screws on the chain sprocket slipped while holding the timing, the entire cam timing could be offset.

A common pitfall in this specific repair is assuming that because the engine turns partially, the timing is intact. The 150-degree rotation limit indicates that one or more pistons are striking open valves as they approach TDC. To confirm this without removing the cam covers immediately, you can try to identify the TDC mark on the crankshaft sprocket while observing the camshaft positions. If the camshafts are not locked and the engine is turned until it binds, note the position of the cam lobes relative to their journals. If a lobe is pointing upward (open valve) when the corresponding piston is near its highest point, you have your diagnosis.

Given that you possess the sixteen-volume Porsche shop manual, consult the section on timing chain installation and removal. It will likely specify the exact procedure for locking the camshafts to prevent rotation during reassembly or inspection. If the cams are not locked, you must assume they are free to rotate unless physically constrained by a tool.

If the timing marks appear aligned but the engine still binds, consider that the chain might have jumped on a sprocket tooth. This is particularly likely if the intermediate shaft bearing was compromised, as a loose bearing can allow the sprocket to slip under tension. In such cases, simply realigning the marks and re-tensioning the chain may not be sufficient; you must ensure the camshaft and crankshaft sprockets are locked in their correct positions before attempting to rotate the engine again.

Avoid forcing the engine further without a definitive diagnosis of which cylinder is causing the interference. If the timing is indeed off by even a single tooth, the valve events will shift significantly enough to cause contact. The safest path forward, while you avoid full disassembly if possible, is to remove the exhaust and cam covers to visually inspect the chain alignment and sprocket marks while the engine is stationary. This allows you to verify that no teeth have skipped and that the intermediate shaft bearing is seating correctly without excessive play.

Once the timing is confirmed correct and the cams are properly aligned with their respective TDC positions, lock the camshafts in place using the appropriate locking tool or method described in your shop manual. Only then should you attempt to rotate the engine through its full 720-degree cycle to ensure smooth operation before reinstalling the remaining components.
